title: How any business can call audit in 4 steps
summary: Performing a call audit doesn’t have to be difficult. Here’s how to get started as a small business owner.
body_markdown:
So your team members are taking customer calls. Great! But making sure those calls meet your standards? That’s where it can get tricky. Even if you have[call handling](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-handling/) guidelines, it’s hard to know whether every customer gets the same level of excellent service, especially if you have a high call volume.


That’s why savvy small businesses turn to call auditing to monitor past conversations and find ways to improve. And no, call auditing isn’t just for big call centers. Small businesses can — and should — audit calls to deliver consistent experiences, improve[customer service efficiency](https://www.quo.com/blog/customer-service-efficiency/) , and keep customers happy.


In this guide, you’ll learn how to run a call audit in four steps, how to take action on what you find, and why small businesses use tools like Quo to deliver better customer experiences at scale.


##


**What is a call audit?**


A call audit is when you listen to past calls to figure out what’s working — and what’s not — with your customer service.


Once you’ve finished your audit, you can create an audit report that lists key findings, trends, and ways to improve, so you can:


- Train your team more effectively
- Fix recurring issues before they cost you business
- Make smarter decisions about how you handle customer calls.


Think about the last time you called the vet when your pet was sick and the person on the other end was calm, helpful, and clear. Calls like that don’t happen by accident. They’re usually audited behind the scenes and shared internally so customers get that experience each time they call.


##


**How to perform a call audit without a call center budget**


Call center blogs make the call auditing process sound intimidating and complex — especially if you have to sift through jargon like “BPO optimization” and “QM calibration.”


But auditing calls can be simple and doable for small businesses. It just takes[listening to calls](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-listening/) , scoring them against a checklist, and identifying key takeaways to spot patterns.


Here’s the four-step process you need to get started:


### **1. Pick a few sample calls**


Reviewing every business call can take a lot of time — and as a small business owner, you probably don’t have much time lying around. So start with something less intimidating, like samples of calls from across your business.


Here are several suggestions for picking good samples:


- A mix of everyday inbound and outbound calls — selected at random — to capture a range of typical customer interactions
- Calls from unhappy customers to spot service gaps
- Sales team call recordings to find missed upsells or coaching opportunities


The number of samples you should aim for depends on the size of your team. That said, three to four calls per team member per month is usually a solid start.


You also don’t have to listen to every call to pick samples.[Call tags](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/call-tagging) can give you the context you need. For example, you can track[customer sentiment](https://www.quo.com/blog/customer-sentiment/) ,[call drivers](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-drivers/) , or specific scenarios. Then, filter calls by tags to narrow down topics and build a well-rounded review set.


Quo users can also tap into[call views](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/team-collaboration/guides/call-views-coaching) to filter calls by team member or date. That way, you can pick samples from a diverse pool of reps over the past days or weeks.


We cover the nuts and bolts of this in our guide on[how to filter calls for managers](https://www.quo.com/blog/filter-call-for-managers/) .


### **2. Use a simple QA scorecard**


A[quality assurance, or QA, scorecard](https://www.quo.com/blog/customer-service-scorecard/) communicates to your team what “good” looks like on a call. It keeps ratings unbiased and prevents favoritism. It also adds structure to each session so you can evaluate all recordings against the same[call-quality](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-quality/) standards.


Here are a few basic and impactful items to score:


- **Greeting.** Was it friendly and professional?
- **Security checkpoints.** Are team members handling customer data securely?
- **Issue handling.** Did they solve the customer’s problem?
- **Upsell/cross-sell, if relevant.** Did they identify an opportunity to offer additional relevant products, services, or solutions?
- **Script adherence.** How closely did they follow the recommended script? In what ways did they go off-script?
- **Closing.** Did they end the call politely and make sure the customer was happy?


This is what a sample scorecard would look like:


Criteria Description Rating scale


Greeting and closing Did the rep start and end with a professional greeting script? Yes/No


Compliance and security Did the rep follow company guidelines for compliance and security, like verifying identity, obtaining necessary consent, and following required protocols? Yes/No


Empathy Did the rep acknowledge the customer’s issue and empathize with their concerns? Yes/No


Tone Was a professional and helpful tone used throughout the conversation? Five-point scale


Effectiveness Did the rep identify the customer’s issue properly? Were they able to resolve the issue if possible? Yes/No


Spelling and grammar Were responses clear and free from grammar and spelling errors? Five-point scale


Solution and follow-up Did the rep offer a complete and accurate solution? If follow-up was required, did the rep create a note to do this? Yes/No


Timely responses Did the rep send responses in a timely fashion? Yes/No


Download the[customer service quality assurance scorecard .](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1_1cMnadfmCwNwakWwiWHEN7DRYHI8AO0ycUFhXvwTTE/edit?gid=0#gid=0)


Be sure to calibrate the scorecard by meeting with your team and defining what the scores mean. For example, what counts as three points for empathy versus five points?


Review the scorecard at least twice a year. Products and scripts change over time, and so do security and customer service standards.


💡 **Pro tip.** Base your[customer service quality assurance](https://www.quo.com/blog/customer-service-quality-assurance/) checklist on the key performance indicators, or KPIs, that matter most to your business. For example, if one of your goals is fewer callbacks, score whether team members fully resolve customer issues the first time.


### **3. Listen and score**


Now that you’ve got your samples and scorecard, it’s time to go through your call recordings. You can easily pull these from a business phone system like Quo. Just make sure you follow all best practices for[legally recording phone calls](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-legally-record-phone-calls/) .


Short on time? Use[call transcripts](https://www.quo.com/features/call-transcriptions) and AI summaries to get up to speed faster and reference specific parts of a conversation as needed.


And one more thing — don’t sweat the small stuff. A slight fumble probably isn’t worth docking points if it isn’t affecting customer satisfaction. Instead, focus on patterns and the customer experience so your feedback is valuable and actionable, not nitpicky.


💡 **Not sure how to quantify your customer’s experience?** You can read our[call disposition](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-disposition/) guide about how to categorize the outcome of a call.


### **4. Spot patterns across multiple calls**


Once you’ve completed a few call reviews, take a step back and look at your scorecards. What trends or topics keep popping up? Are there things you can address with[customer service coaching](https://www.quo.com/blog/customer-service-coaching/) ?


For example, maybe your team nails the “friendly service” guideline but tends to miss follow-ups. Or maybe new hires keep forgetting to mention your cancellation policy, which could become a bigger problem if clients need to reschedule.


The more employees and recordings you have to review, the harder it may be to get a good picture. This can be a big time saver for small businesses that don’t have a lot of bandwidth.

Which leads to our final point:


##


**Next steps: How to take action on your** **audit results** ****


So you’ve combed through recordings, filled out scorecards, and found recurring patterns across multiple calls. All that’s left is to create a plan of action.


Here’s how to put those call audit outcomes to good use:


- **Update scripts, FAQs, or website copy.** If customers keep asking the same questions, you might add more entries to your FAQ or a dedicated audio recording to your[IVR](https://www.quo.com/blog/what-is-ivr/) or phone menu. You could also tweak call scripts to make them more accessible, like simplifying language around pricing and billing.
- **Make coaching plans.** Adjust your[call coaching](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-coaching/) approach to individual employees. For example, if a new hire is jumping into promotions too early, you could have them focus on solving the customer’s issue first during the next five calls.
- **Share wins with your team.** Your team deserves to know what they’re doing well just as much as what they need to improve. If you’re a Quo user, you can use internal threads to highlight great calls and tag team members with real-time praise.


##


**Call metrics for small businesses**


Here are a few common metrics small business owners track:


- **Increase**[first call resolution](https://www.quo.com/blog/first-call-resolution/) **, or FCR, rates.** More customers get their questions answered on the first call.
- [Shorter average handle time](https://www.quo.com/blog/average-handle-time/) **.** Calls end faster because customers get answers sooner.
- **Higher customer satisfaction scores, or CSAT.** More customers feel satisfied with the service they received.
- **Lower customer effort score.** It takes customers less effort to get what they need.
- **Lower missed call rate** . Fewer customers are sent to voicemail or hang up without reaching someone on your team.


##


**Call audit best practices**


A good call auditing process can do wonders for a rep’s performance, call quality, and customer experience. Conversely, a bad call audit can be worse than not having one at all. Here are some tips on how to keep yours on the right track.


### **Establish a regular call audit schedule**


To continually improve your customer experience, run call audits regularly and consistently. So, how often? The cadence will depend on the size of your team, call volume, and how much they need to improve. You should also communicate the schedule to your team. This will help build trust and a culture of professional growth. Surprise reviews can hurt morale and increase your team’s anxiety.


### **Host call calibration sessions**


How do you define a “good” call? That’s what a[call calibration](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-calibration/) session is for. Get everyone, from managers to reps, into a room and go over the evaluation criteria. Review different scenarios and discuss the standards by which a call should be scored. Your people will have a better idea of performance expectations. Customers will also have a consistent, top-notch experience with every team member.


To ensure consistency, you might add recurring audit sessions to your calendar each month. Have multiple phone numbers to juggle, like sales versus customer support? You can also delegate auditing to a more experienced rep.


### **Focus on the issue you’re trying to fix**


Some metrics matter more than others, and that should be defined by your current goal. Need to improve call handling times? Focus on those during call auditing and coaching sessions. Call audit goals can also shift over time, and that’s ok.


### **Keep detailed records of each call**


Make sure to keep records as complete as you can. Not just the call recording, but also the related transactions, messages, and team notes. This will help with the call auditing process so the auditor has the whole picture.

##


**FAQs**


****Why should small businesses audit their calls?****


Four benefits of call auditing for small business owners include:


– **Spot issues early.** Regularly auditing calls helps you catch small mistakes before they cause bigger problems. For example, if you notice a new hire forgetting to mention your cancellation policy, you can flag and fix it before missed appointments start costing you money


– **Keep customers happy and coming back.** You can use call audits for quality monitoring, which means finding and correcting hiccups in customer service, like inefficient call routing. That way, you can improve operational efficiency and keep customers from courting competitors.


– **Maintain quality while you grow.** Maintaining support quality can be a major challenge as you scale. But just because you’re growing doesn’t mean call quality has to slip. You can use audit findings to identify performance improvement opportunities and boost your customer satisfaction scores.


– **Catch compliance issues before they catch you.** Are your reps asking permission before recording? Or following scripts before collecting sensitive info? Regular audits can help you spot slip-ups before they become bigger problems.


****What’s the difference between a call audit and call monitoring?****


Call monitoring is listening to live and recorded calls to check whether they meet your service-level quality standards . This usually involves[call monitoring software](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-monitoring-software/) and[call listening](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-listening/) tools like automatic call recording, AI call tagging, and group calling.


Call auditing is reviewing completed calls against specific criteria to spot patterns, flag issues, and improve performance with valuable insights.


****What is the role of a call auditor?****


A call auditor listens to past calls and conducts the audit process. As a small business owner, this could be you or another team member in a managerial position.


Need to perform call center audits? You probably have different business needs. You might need to delegate tasks to a CX or call center manager who can watch over your team or department.


****Do I need contact center software to audit calls?****


All you need to audit calls is a small business phone system that stores copies of call recordings and transcripts, like Quo.


But if you’re a contact center that needs to track call center performance for rep training, you may need a dedicated software provider.


**Is call auditing required by law?**


In certain industries, yes. Financial services, healthcare, insurance, and debt collection all require a documented call auditing process that covers recording consent, disclosure scripts, and data handling. The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, or PCI DSS, also requires an audit trail.
